messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus had always been someone who prided himself on control — over his systems, his schedules, his carefully ordered life. At thirty-four, he was a competent database administrator at a mid-sized logistics firm in Columbus, Ohio, the kind of man who kept redundant backups and never missed a deadline. Then, during a routine afternoon at his desk, he felt a tightening across his chest that he initially dismissed as stress. By evening he could not draw a full breath. His wife drove him to the emergency room, where the next several hours dissolved into a blur of oxygen masks, IV lines threaded into his arm, the cold press of electrodes, and a physician's careful voice explaining that a pulmonary embolism had nearly killed him. He lay in that hospital bed for four days, watching nurses approach with syringes, listening to the rhythmic beeping of monitors, and feeling — for the first time in his adult life — that his own body was a place he could not trust.

In the months that followed, Marcus's recovery was technically successful. Medically, he was cleared. Psychologically, something had not resolved. His body, he had come to believe, was still in the grip of that emergency room — still braced for the moment the air would stop coming. He noticed this most acutely at his workstation, where long hours of sedentary concentration would sometimes produce a faint pressure in his chest. Immediately his attention would narrow onto his own breathing, and within seconds what had been a mild sensation would become a terrifying one: his chest tight, his heart loud, his breath short and ragged. These episodes left him shaking, convinced each time that the embolism had returned. His body felt permanently tensed, as though standing sentry against a threat that might announce itself at any moment through a skipped heartbeat or an unusual tightness in his lungs. The fear, the horror, the physical alarm — these were not occasional visitors. They were the background hum of his daily existence.

It was from within this state of chronic physiological vigilance that Marcus began building his own system of management — one that made complete sense to him even as it quietly dismantled his life. He stopped exercising entirely. Running, he reasoned, would accelerate his heart and constrict his breathing, and he could not afford to confuse those sensations with another clot. He began controlling his food intake with rigid precision, eating small, carefully measured portions, because he had decided that weight and exertion placed demands on a cardiovascular system he no longer trusted. He cancelled a follow-up cardiology appointment, then another, and eventually stopped engaging with any medical setting altogether — no examinations, no blood draws, no waiting rooms with their antiseptic smell and the soft squeak of nurses' shoes. These strategies felt like protection. What he did not see, for a long time, was that they were also a cage.

Because his avoidance was so thorough, Marcus never had the opportunity to learn that his body could tolerate movement, that a racing heart from a brisk walk was not a harbinger of catastrophe. Instead, the absence of any corrective experience left his nervous system exactly where it had been the night of the embolism. And the avoidance itself became a source of triggers: on the rare occasions when something slipped through — a colleague mentioning a hospital visit, a needle glimpsed in a television drama, a moment of breathlessness when he climbed the stairs too quickly — the reaction was immediate and overwhelming. His body flooded with the same alarm it had felt in the emergency room, which only confirmed his belief that the danger was real and ongoing, and that the avoidance had to be maintained, even intensified. His restricted eating and sedentary routine, meant to protect him, kept his threat system perpetually primed.

His divorce was finalised eight months ago. His ex-wife had grown exhausted by the restrictions that had gradually colonised their shared life. Marcus came to his first session quiet and precise, describing his symptoms the way he might describe a corrupted database — methodically, with a faint undertone of shame. What finally brought him was a performance review at work, where his manager had noted increasing withdrawal from the team. What he feared most was that he had already passed the point of return. What he hoped, though he said it carefully, was that he had not.
